name: Editorial Consumer Brand Pitch
description: For premium consumer and lifestyle brands: warm ivory space, editorial serif typography, cognac accents, tactile photography, and refined retail evidence.
style_guide:
# Editorial Consumer Fundraising

## Design intent

Create a premium consumer-brand fundraising deck that feels like an editorial brand book with investor discipline. The mood is warm, tactile, quiet, and assured: generous ivory space, high-contrast serif claims, restrained cognac accents, fine rules, elegant product or lifestyle photography, and precisely edited commercial evidence. The presentation should communicate taste and brand desirability without sacrificing market logic, operating clarity, or numerical credibility.

Every page should balance one memorable proposition with one organized evidence structure. Let typography and whitespace do most of the work; use photography only when it adds real product, customer, or brand context. Preserve the visual language shown by the previews, but never copy their company, people, product names, facts, metrics, dates, quotes, labels, or slide sequence. Preview images are UI-only references; this written guide is the complete authoring authority.

## Non-negotiable page grammar

- Use a fixed `1280 × 720 px` canvas in a 16:9 ratio.
- Keep `64 px` left and right safe margins and `42–52 px` top and bottom safe margins. No text, chart label, or photographic subject may be clipped.
- Use a 12-column grid with `20–24 px` gutters. Align headlines, image edges, card edges, chart baselines, dividers, and footer metadata to shared columns.
- Use generous negative space. Ordinary pages should contain one dominant headline region and one evidence region, not a dashboard of unrelated tiles.
- Content pages use a compact top metadata line: `NN — SECTION NAME` at top-left, current page/total pages at top-right, and a thin warm-gray rule beneath.
- Place the main editorial headline below the header with enough separation to read as a distinct field. Use a short serif statement, normally one to three lines.
- Reserve the bottom edge for a quiet source, note, or page count only. Do not build a heavy footer bar.
- Use both light and dark pages deliberately. Light ivory is the default; a dark reverse page is reserved for market strategy, a major transition, or another analytically dense chapter that benefits from contrast.

## Color system

### Light mode

- Warm ivory canvas: `#F4F0E8`. Use as the default slide background.
- Soft paper panel: `#EAE2D3`. Use for market callouts, quote bands, secondary analysis, and understated grouping.
- Clean white: `#FCFBF8`. Use sparingly for comparison cards or KPI cards that need separation from the ivory canvas.
- Editorial ink: `#1B1714`. Use for primary headlines, key values, body emphasis, dark cards, and chart anchors.
- Body umber: `#51483F`. Use for explanatory copy, labels, and axes.
- Quiet taupe: `#9A9084`. Use for secondary metadata, inactive chart marks, borders, and reference lines.
- Hairline beige: `#D8CFC1`. Use for one-pixel dividers, table rules, and chart grids.

### Accents

- Cognac: `#9A4A12`. This is the primary brand accent. Use for italic headline phrases, active bars, category markers, selected values, and section metadata.
- Burnished ochre: `#C6A16F`. Use for secondary charts, market tiers, timelines, and warm comparison states.
- Botanical sage: `#647E64`. Use sparingly for positive performance, repeat behavior, sustainability, talent, or a fourth allocation category.
- Deep chocolate: `#211C18`. Use for a featured card or the full dark reverse page.
- Reverse cream: `#F1EADF`. Use for primary text on Deep chocolate.

### Color discipline

- Warm ivory, Editorial ink, and Cognac define the identity. Ochre and sage support specific data meanings.
- Keep light pages mostly ivory and dark pages mostly Deep chocolate. Do not add saturated modern UI colors such as electric blue, neon green, or bright violet.
- Use Cognac in small, high-value moments rather than as a large background fill. A colored italic phrase, one card, or one chart series is enough.
- Pair every color-coded category with a direct label, value, position, or shape. Never use color as the only encoding.
- Avoid decorative gradients. Photographs may contain natural tonal variation, but authored backgrounds and charts use flat colors.

## Typography

- Display font: `Georgia` or `Times New Roman`. Use a high-contrast serif for the title, decisive claims, large values, founder names, and short editorial annotations.
- Supporting font: `Arial` or another common system sans-serif. Use it for metadata, body copy, charts, tables, captions, and operational detail.
- Cover title: `52–64 px`, serif, weight `400–500`, line-height `1.02–1.1`. Keep it to two or three lines.
- Content-page claim: `38–52 px`, serif, weight `400–500`, line-height `1.04–1.14`. It should read like an editorial conclusion, not a generic topic label.
- Highlight phrase: inherit the headline size, use serif italic and Cognac or Burnished ochre. Highlight one phrase, not every keyword.
- Section metadata: `9–11 px`, sans-serif, weight `600–700`, uppercase when the language supports it, letter-spacing `2.5–4 px`, Cognac.
- Hero metric: `36–56 px`, serif, weight `400–500`. KPI value: `30–42 px`, serif.
- Panel or product-family title: `22–30 px`, serif. Card title: `15–18 px`, sans-serif, weight `700`, or `19–24 px` serif when the card is editorial rather than operational.
- Body copy: `12–15 px`, sans-serif, weight `400–500`, line-height `1.45–1.6`, Body umber.
- Quotes, mantras, and short customer language: `16–22 px`, serif italic, line-height `1.4–1.55`. Use only grounded quotes or clearly labeled synthesis.
- Chart labels, table text, captions, and footnotes: `9–12 px`, sans-serif. Never use this size for essential explanatory content.
- For CJK output, pair a common system CJK serif for display with a common system CJK sans-serif for support. Preserve hierarchy and restraint rather than forcing Latin letter-spacing or italic conventions.

## Photography and image treatment

- Prefer premium product still life, tactile materials, natural ingredients, customer rituals, retail environments, packaging details, founder portraits, and brand-relevant lifestyle scenes. Images must be grounded visual assets available to the current page.
- Use warm natural light, quiet neutral backgrounds, soft directional shadows, restrained saturation, and visible material texture. The image should feel photographed, not rendered as glossy advertising CGI.
- Use one dominant photograph or a very small curated set. Avoid collages of many unrelated images.
- Crop deliberately around the subject and preserve clear negative space. Keep skin, packaging, labels, and product proportions natural.
- Do not fabricate product packaging, logos, customer portraits, store imagery, or endorsements. If no suitable grounded photograph exists, use a typographic composition, an abstract flat color field, or a restrained evidence diagram instead.
- Do not put body copy over busy image detail. When text and image share a page, assign them separate grid regions or use a quiet solid overlay with strong contrast.
- No rounded photo masks, heavy color filters, artificial blur, sticker effects, or decorative image frames. Rectangular edge-to-edge crops and clean paper margins are preferred.

## Components and editorial hierarchy

- Light cards use Clean white or Soft paper, square corners or at most `2–4 px` radius, no shadow, and either no border or a one-pixel Hairline beige border.
- A featured card may reverse to Deep chocolate with Reverse cream text and Burnished ochre metadata. Use only one such card in a row.
- Thin vertical or horizontal rules create structure. Avoid thick bars, rounded pills, and application-style controls.
- Editorial indices use `01`, `02`, `03` in a large light ochre serif, followed by a short bold label and two to four lines of evidence.
- KPI strips contain three or four equal blocks with a small metadata label, one large serif value, and one short comparison or interpretation.
- Position maps use two fine axes, direct quadrant labels, quiet competitor marks, and one Cognac focal mark for the current company.
- Timelines use a single fine line, small filled nodes, date labels above or below, and short milestone descriptions.
- Allocation bars use flat adjacent segments in Deep chocolate, Cognac, Ochre, Sage, and Quiet taupe. Pair the bar with a direct legend, amounts, and percentages.
- Use short italic closing lines or mantras sparingly at the bottom of a page. They reinforce the thesis but never substitute for evidence.

## Charts and commercial evidence

- Charts should feel like editorial figures, not software dashboards. Use minimal axes, hairline grids, direct labels, and substantial whitespace.
- Prefer simple bars for growth, lines for repeat or cohort behavior, stacked bars for allocation or channel mix, market nesting for TAM/SAM/SOM, and a two-axis map for positioning.
- Use Cognac as the primary series, Editorial ink for a current or target state, Ochre for a secondary series, Sage for positive comparison, and Quiet taupe for a benchmark or inactive series.
- On dark pages, use Reverse cream for critical labels, Burnished ochre for active values, and low-contrast warm gray for grids.
- Directly label the decisive values. Every number must include unit, period, actual/estimate/target status, and source or evidence context where applicable.
- Keep tables light and sparse: thin horizontal rules, no heavy outer border, short row labels, and right-aligned comparable values.
- Do not invent market sizes, pricing, customer behavior, revenue, retention, margin, CAC, growth, founder credentials, funding amounts, or channel performance to complete the visual.

## Adaptable composition families

These are composition tendencies, not executable templates, fixed slide requirements, or permission to reuse preview content. Select only the structure that best serves the current Outline Entry.

- Cover: use a 38/62 or 42/58 split. Place a sparse ivory editorial title block on the left and one dominant warm still-life or brand image on the right. Include a small round or confidentiality label and a restrained presenter/company metadata row.
- Consumer insight: place one large editorial claim at the top. Use a tall lifestyle photograph on the lower-left, a short grounded quote or synthesis nearby, three numbered insight columns, and one quiet opportunity band.
- Product portfolio and positioning: use a wide claim, one product photograph, two or three tall family cards, and a compact positioning map. Make one family card dark to establish the hero tier.
- Market and channel strategy: use the dark reverse canvas. Place a large market claim above a 4/8 split with a compact market-size visual on the left and channel-mix bars or strategic actions on the right.
- Traction and economics: use the light canvas, a row of four KPI cards, one dominant growth chart, and a smaller cohort or repeat curve plus a compact operating table.
- Team, expansion, and funds: split the lower page into a founder or leadership column and a wider plan column. Use a horizontal timeline above a segmented use-of-funds bar, with one restrained product image or prior-backer note only when grounded.
- Brand story: use one sparse claim, a short manifesto or set of principles, and a single tactile image. Keep commercial implications explicit rather than creating a purely aesthetic mood board.
- Go-to-market: use a channel sequence, retail footprint map, or acquisition-to-repeat flow with direct economics. Avoid turning channel logos into decoration.
- Competition: use one positioning map or comparison table with a concise implication. Competitors stay neutral; the current brand is the only Cognac focal point.
- Closing ask: use a spacious light or dark page with the brand thesis, funding ask, use of funds, next milestone, and contact path. Do not repeat every KPI.

## Allowed variation

- Preserve the ivory/ink/cognac palette, serif-led hierarchy, fine rules, editorial spacing, and restrained evidence style across the deck.
- Alternate photo-led pages with data-led pages so the presentation breathes. Do not require photography on every slide.
- Use a dark reverse page as a chapter accent, normally no more than one in three or four pages. The transition must correspond to a real narrative or analytical shift.
- Layouts may be symmetric or asymmetric, but their edges remain disciplined and their reading order obvious.
- Warm imagery may vary with the actual consumer category: beauty, food, fashion, home, wellness, or another premium brand context. Preserve the quiet editorial treatment without forcing skincare motifs onto unrelated content.
- Adapt line breaks, emphasis, and font pairing to the confirmed output language. Use italic only where the script and installed fonts support it legibly.

## Avoid

- Do not reproduce preview companies, people, products, prices, market sizes, traction, dates, quotes, credentials, investors, or funding terms unless grounded in the current Workspace.
- Do not turn the deck into a generic beauty, skincare, or beige lifestyle template when the actual subject is another consumer category. Transfer the visual grammar, not the preview content.
- Do not use SaaS-style rounded cards, neon accents, glassmorphism, glowing gradients, 3D charts, icon grids, or dense dashboards.
- Do not use script fonts, ornamental calligraphy, or long italic paragraphs. The serif should feel editorial and readable, not decorative.
- Do not place text over busy photography, use low-contrast taupe for essential copy, or shrink evidence below readable size.
- Do not overuse the dark reverse mode, product photography, italic accents, or Cognac. Restraint is central to the style.
- If evidence or imagery is missing, omit the unsupported detail, generalize the statement, or use a clearly labeled `TBD` or localized equivalent.
